claim: The paragraph in proof/F4_GE_52_HAND_PROOF.md that begins 'Theorem 1 holds for every N, not only N = 51' is an incomplete proof. Its first unjustified inference is the sentence asserting that (*), (R1)-(R3) and the rounding lemma hold verbatim at every order once gamma_u is redefined as the number of vertices y with q_y >= 9 and u not in Q_y. The conclusion of that paragraph is true by the argument written in this report, which is the auditor's proof and not a repair declared to be the printed text: in every S_4 tournament, on any number of vertices, every tight pair P satisfies J(P) >= 3. This verdict covers that every-order claim. It does not certify the N = 51 write-up of Theorem 1, it does not prove J >= 5 on 52 vertices, and it does not solve Erdős 902.
definitions: T is a tournament on N vertices with property S_4: every set of 4 vertices has a dominator outside it. D(X) is the set of vertices outside X that beat every member of X. A pair P is tight when |D(P)| = 11. Write R = D(P), O = V \ (P union R), Q_y = R intersect N^-(y) and q_y = |Q_y| for y in O. For r in R write d^-(r) = 25 + j_r and J(P) = sum_{r in R} j_r. c(u, v) is the number of vertices of R that beat both u and v. A 5-vertex is a y in O with q_y = 5; a 6-vertex has q_y = 6; a big vertex has q_y >= 9. For u in R, alpha_u, beta_u and gamma_u count the 5-vertices, 6-vertices and big vertices that beat u. k(u, v) and m(u, v) count the 5-vertices and 6-vertices that beat both u and v. s(u, v) is the sum of |D({u, v, w})| - 5 over the nine vertices w in R \ {u, v}. N_4(u) is the number of v different from u with c(u, v) + m(u, v) >= 4. Lambda(q) = 10 - C(10 - q, 2), with the binomial coefficient zero when the top is smaller than the bottom. Lemma I of research/LEMMAS.md is the pair of identities #{y in O: r not in Q_y} = 20 + j_r and sum_y (q_y - 5) = 6N - 298 - J, under the hypotheses checked in the argument. Lemma S1 is not used.
argument:
Diagnosis of the printed paragraph. The sentence that the in-neighbours of r in O are exactly the y with r not in Q_y, and that there are d^-(r) - 5 = 20 + j_r of them, is correct for every N: r beats both vertices of P, T[R] is 5-regular, and Lemma T gives d^-(r) = 25 + j_r. The identity (*) follows from that count, because its printed derivation uses the count only through (I1). The next clause does not follow. (R1) as printed is proved under Lemma P, whose profile is one heavy vertex, no q in {7, 8}, and at most two 6-vertices, and whose triple count uses |O| = 38. The symbol gamma_u does not occur in (R1). Redefining it does not re-derive the outside contribution when several vertices have q >= 9, and it does not exclude q in {7, 8}. (R2), (R3) and the rounding lemma are derived from that form of (R1), so they are not available verbatim either. That is the first unjustified inference. Later sentences have the same character: 'no 6-vertex' is the first half of Step 2, not Step 1, and 'Steps 3-5 are unchanged' cites text written for a single vertex y*. The paragraph is therefore incomplete. It is not a false proof: the same bound is proved from scratch below.

Inputs, re-read from proof/ERDOS902_PROOF.md and N-free. Lemma 1.2: if |A| <= 3, D(A) is undominated. If some z beat every vertex of D(A), then A union {z} would have a dominator w outside it, forcing w in D(A) and both z -> w and w -> z. An undominated set has more than 4 vertices, so every triple has at least 5 dominators. Lemma 1.3: for a pair P with R = D(P) and y not in P, D(P union {y}) = R intersect N^-(y), so q_y >= 5, and T[R] has minimum in-degree at least 5. A tight pair has |R| = 11 = 2*5 + 1, so the in-degrees inside T[R] sum to C(11, 2) = 55 = 11*5 and T[R] is 5-regular. Lemma 2.1: fix r in R. The C(10, 2) = 45 triples of R through r contribute at least 225 dominator incidences. The five vertices of R that beat r contribute 6 triples each, hence 30. Every other dominator lies in O, and there are d^-(r) - 5 of them. Each is beaten by at least 5 vertices of R, so it beats at most 6 vertices of R, one of them r, and dominates at most C(5, 2) = 10 of the triples. Thus 225 <= 30 + 10(d^-(r) - 5), so d^-(r) >= 24.5, hence d^-(r) >= 25 and every j_r is a nonnegative integer. If N < 13 there is no room for P and an 11-set R, so there is no tight pair and the claim is vacuous. Assume from here that P is tight.

Lemma I, hypotheses checked. d^+(r) = N - 1 - d^-(r) = N - 26 - j_r. Seven out-neighbours of r already lie in P union R, so r has N - 33 - j_r out-neighbours in O. Then |O| - (N - 33 - j_r) = 20 + j_r vertices of O beat r. Summing the opposite direction, sum_y q_y = sum_r (N - 33 - j_r) = 11N - 363 - J, and subtracting 5|O| = 5N - 65 gives sum_y (q_y - 5) = 6N - 298 - J.

The inequality (*). The same 45 triples satisfy sum |D(U)| = 30 + sum_{y: r not in Q_y} C(10 - q_y, 2). There are 20 + j_r terms in the sum, so sum |D(U)| = 230 + 10 j_r - sum lambda(q_y). Comparing with 225 gives sum lambda(q_y) <= 5 + 10 j_r. The values used below are lambda(5) = 0, lambda(6) = 4, lambda(7) = 7, lambda(8) = 9, and lambda(9) = lambda(10) = 10. A vertex with q_y = 11 does not beat r.

Proof of J >= 3. Assume J <= 2. If some q_y = 7, each of the four vertices r outside Q_y has lambda at least 7 in (*), so 7 <= 5 + 10 j_r and j_r >= 1, hence J >= 4. If some q_y = 8, each of the three vertices outside Q_y has 9 <= 5 + 10 j_r, so j_r >= 1 and J >= 3. Both contradict J <= 2. Every q_y therefore lies in {5, 6, 9, 10, 11}.

Pair excess in this profile. A vertex of R dominates {u, v, w} only if it beats u and v. There are c(u, v) such vertices, and each beats exactly three further vertices of R, because its out-degree in R is 5. A vertex y in O dominates {u, v, w} exactly when y beats u, y beats v and y beats w, that is, when u, v and w all lie outside Q_y. If y beats both u and v, the number of admissible w is |R \ Q_y| - 2 = 9 - q_y. That number is 4, 3, 0 for q = 5, 6, 9. A vertex with q >= 10 misses at most one vertex of R, so it does not beat both u and v. Therefore s(u, v) = 3c(u, v) + 4k(u, v) + 3m(u, v) - 45.

Sum and congruence. Summing over the ten vertices v different from u, (I3) gives sum c(u, v) = 20: each of the five in-neighbours of u in R has four further out-neighbours in R. Each 5-vertex that beats u beats five further vertices of R, and each 6-vertex that beats u beats four further vertices, so sum_v k = 5 alpha_u and sum_v m = 4 beta_u. The sum of s is 60 + 20 alpha_u + 12 beta_u - 450. Substitute alpha_u = 20 + j_u - beta_u - gamma_u to obtain sum_v s(u, v) = 10 + 20 j_u - 8 beta_u - 20 gamma_u. Modulo 4, the term 4k vanishes, 3c is congruent to -c, 3m is congruent to -m, and -45 is congruent to 3, so s(u, v) is congruent to 3 - c(u, v) - m(u, v).

Rounding without a bound on the number of 6-vertices. Let x = c + m and let s >= 0 be an integer congruent to 3 - x modulo 4. If x <= 3, then 3 - x is nonnegative and is the least such residue, so s >= 3 - x. If x >= 4, any integer strictly smaller than 7 - x and in the same residue class is at most 3 - x <= -1. Thus every nonnegative s in the class satisfies s >= 7 - x, whether or not 7 - x itself is positive. Equivalently, s >= 3 - c - m + 4 when x >= 4. Summing over v, sum s >= 30 - 20 - 4 beta_u + 4 N_4(u). Compare with the earlier evaluation: 10 + 20 j_u - 8 beta_u - 20 gamma_u >= 10 - 4 beta_u + 4 N_4(u), which simplifies to beta_u + 5 gamma_u + N_4(u) <= 5 j_u.

No 6-vertex. If j_u = 0, the rounding inequality forces beta_u = gamma_u = N_4(u) = 0. A 6-vertex beats five vertices of R, and none of those five can have j = 0. Each has j >= 1, so J >= 5, contradicting J <= 2. Hence there is no 6-vertex. Every remaining non-5 vertex is big, beta_u = 0 and m(u, v) = 0 for every pair, and the rounding inequality reduces to gamma_u <= j_u. With Gamma = sum_u gamma_u = sum_{big y} |R \ Q_y|, one has Gamma <= J.

Divisibility. Only big vertices contribute to the excess, and a big vertex that beats t vertices of R has q = 11 - t and excess 6 - t. The excess sum is 6m - Gamma, where m is the number of big vertices. Lemma I says this equals 6N - 298 - J. Rearrangement gives 6(m - N + 50) = 2 - J + Gamma. The right side is an integer, at least 2 - J >= 0 and at most 2 - J + J = 2. The only multiple of 6 in {0, 1, 2} is 0. Therefore J = 2, Gamma = 0 and m = N - 50. Gamma = 0 means every big vertex has Q_y = R. If N < 50 this value of m is negative, which is impossible. In every remaining case the big vertices beat nobody in R, and every y that beats a given s in R is a 5-vertex.

The N = 51 case split, now free of |O| = 38. For u with j_u = 0, beta_u = gamma_u = 0, so sum_v s(u, v) = 10. Also N_4(u) = 0 and m = 0, so c(u, v) <= 3 and s(u, v) >= 3 - c(u, v). The lower bounds sum to 30 - 20 = 10. Equality holds termwise: s(u, v) = 3 - c(u, v). The pair formula then gives 4k(u, v) = 48 - 4c(u, v), so k = 12 - c. The dominators of {u, v} are the c common in-neighbours in R together with the 5-vertices that beat both, because every big vertex beats nobody in R and there is no 6-vertex. Thus |D({u, v})| = 12 for every v different from such a u.

For an arbitrary s in R, the same description of dominators gives sum_{v different from s} |D({s, v})| = sum c + sum k = 20 + 5 alpha_s. Here alpha_s = 20 + j_s, so the sum equals 120 + 5 j_s.

J = 2 has two integer shapes. If one vertex s has j_s = 2, the other ten vertices have j = 0, each pair from s to them has 12 dominators, and the sum is 120. The preceding formula requires 130. If two vertices s1, s2 have j = 1, the formula at s1 requires sum 125, and the nine pairs from s1 into the j = 0 set contribute 108, so |D({s1, s2})| = 17. Then k = 17 - c and s(s1, s2) = 3c + 4(17 - c) - 45 = 23 - c. Since c <= 4, this is at least 19. On the other hand sum_v s(s1, v) = 10 + 20 = 30. Each triple through s1 is counted twice in that sum, once for each way of ordering its other two vertices, so the 45 triples through s1 have total excess 15. The nine triples through both s1 and s2 are among them and the excesses are nonnegative, so s(s1, s2) <= 15. This contradicts s(s1, s2) >= 19.

Both shapes are impossible, so the assumption J <= 2 is false. Every tight pair satisfies J >= 3.

Hand check of the terminal counts, not used as a step. At J = 2, Gamma = 0 and m = N - 50, the excess identity reads 6(N - 50) = 6N - 300 on both sides. The number of 5-vertices is |O| - m = 37. They contribute 37*6 = 222 incidences of a vertex of R beaten from O, and sum_r (20 + j_r) = 220 + 2 = 222.

evidence.first_unjustified_inference: Hence (*), (R1)-(R3) and the rounding lemma hold verbatim, with gamma_u redefined as a count of y with q_y >= 9 missing u.
evidence.what_does_follow_from_the_in_neighbour_c: (*) and Lemma I, at every N
evidence.what_does_not_follow: (R1), (R2), (R3), the rounding lemma, and the citation of Steps 3-5 as unchanged
evidence.auditor_theorem: Every tight pair in every S_4 tournament satisfies J >= 3
evidence.excluded_under_J_at_most_2: q_y in {7, 8} by (*); q_y = 6 by the rounding lemma plus five positive j-values
evidence.divisibility: 6(m - N + 50) = 2 - J + Gamma, right side an integer in {0, 1, 2}, hence 0, so J = 2, Gamma = 0, m = N - 50, Q_y = R
evidence.case_two_j_equals_1: |D| = 17, s = 23 - c >= 19, while the excess through one endpoint is 15
evidence.terminal_count_check: excess 6N - 300 on both sides; 37 five-vertices give 222 = 220 + J

weaknesses: The status proved applies only to the argument written here. The printed paragraph remains incomplete, and the sentence that Steps 3-5 are unchanged is still not a citation of a matching text: Step 3 in the N = 51 write-up names a single vertex y*. The following paragraph of the same note, lines 213-218, claims the in-degree-25 structural fact for an arbitrary tight pair with no bound on J. Its parenthetical proof invokes the rounding lemma as written, which assumes the N = 51 profile, and that paragraph was not given a proof in this report. Sections 3 and 4 of proof/N52_TIGHT_PAIRS.md, which exclude J = 3 and J = 4 at N = 52, were not audited. The lower bound s >= 7 - x is weak once x >= 8; the argument removes every 6-vertex before the final comparison, so that weak range is not where the contradiction is drawn. No enumeration was run.
next_step: Audit sections 3 and 4 of proof/N52_TIGHT_PAIRS.md, the exclusions of J = 3 and J = 4 at N = 52 that sit on top of J >= 3. Separately, supply a proof of the in-degree-25 structural statement in the paragraph after the every-order claim, the one that allows q_y in {7, 8} and does not assume J <= 2.
relation_to_prior: This verdict covers the every-order paragraph, not the N = 51 case analysis of Theorem 1. research/LEMMAS.md records that extension as open: Lemma P uses |O| = 38, (R1) is not re-derived for several vertices of q >= 9, and Steps 3-5 are asserted for m = N - 50. Lemma I applies, because a tight pair in an S_4 tournament meets its hypotheses, and the identity is re-derived above; the lemma states by itself that it does not force J >= 3. Lemma S1 is not an input. proof/N52_TIGHT_PAIRS.md cites the paragraph for J >= 3 at every order and then claims J >= 5 at N = 52; only the cited input is treated here. The exhausted approach keys are not used. proof/swarm/r1_AUDIT-51.md section 5 is an earlier workspace sketch of a repair with the same bound; it was not used as a lemma.
novelty: The mod-4 case split at one vertex of excess 2, or two of excess 1, is the N = 51 split, and the formal line 6(m - N + 50) = 2 - J + Gamma is the paragraph's own algebra. The part that the paragraph does not contain is the justification that makes the algebra applicable: (*) excludes q in {7, 8} at every order under J <= 2; with several vertices of q >= 9 the pair excess is still 3c + 4k + 3m - 45, because each such vertex contributes 0; s >= 7 - x holds for every x >= 4, so rounding does not need the N = 51 bound of two 6-vertices; and once every heavy in-neighbourhood is forced to be all of R, the arithmetic of Steps 3-5 no longer uses |O| = 38 or a single heavy vertex.
